results.title: RTX A4000 Up 10.8% in GPU Rental Market — Week of June 1 - June 7, 2026 | Ai Mining Co. | Ai Mining Co.
highlights:
Weekly snapshot of GPU rental pricing across 29 marketplaces, June 1 - June 7, 2026. Observable data only — no estimates, no predictions.

By Lucas Zelko• Ai Mining Co.

The RTX A4000 posted the largest week-over-week gain among tracked SKUs, rising 10.8% from $0.22 to $0.25 per GPU-hour across the June 1–7, 2026 observation window. The broader market, however, was sharply divergent rather than directional: AIMC tracked 7,300 observations across 29 reporting marketplaces and 109 distinct GPU SKUs, with meaningful moves distributed across both sides of flat. The RTX 5090 shed 9.2% to $0.84, while the B200 SXM climbed 6.3% to $5.97; the RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell fell 5.2% as the L40 gained 4.8%. No single segment absorbed the pressure uniformly. H100 SXM edged up 1.9% to $3.06, a comparatively muted move against the wider dispersion visible elsewhere. What follows breaks down pricing behavior by GPU family, marketplace concentration, and spread dynamics across the four spotlight segments.

...

- 29 authorized marketplace partners contributed pricing data this week. Full list at aiminingco.com/data-partners.
- Largest week-over-week decliner: RTX 5090 at -9.2% ($0.92 → $0.84 average across covered marketplaces).
- Largest week-over-week gainer: RTX A4000 at +10.8% ($0.22 → $0.25 average across covered marketplaces).

## Headline Movements

| GPU | Last Week Avg | This Week Avg | Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX A4000 | $0.22 | $0.25 | +10.8% |
| RTX 5090 | $0.92 | $0.84 | -9.2% |
| B200 SXM | $5.62 | $5.97 | +6.3% |
| RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell | $1.94 | $1.84 | -5.2% |
| L40 | $0.89 | $0.93 | +4.8% |

...

## Marketplace Activity

This week's data spans 29 marketplaces with 7,300 total listing observations across 109 distinct GPU SKUs.

H100 pricing ranged from $1.00/hour at ionet to $5.49/hour at togetherai across 20 marketplaces.

B200 pricing ranged from $3.50/hour at hyperstack to $9.95/hour at togetherai across 8 marketplaces.

L40S pricing ranged from $0.48/hour at tensordock to $2.48/hour at qubrid across 12 marketplaces.

A100 pricing ranged from $0.75/hour at synpixcloud to $4.22/hour at ovhcloud across 18 marketplaces.

...

The most notable pattern in this week's data is the divergence between professional workstation-class GPUs and high-end consumer or inference-focused cards. AIMC's data shows the RTX A4000 posting the week's largest gain at +10.8%, moving from $0.22 to $0.25 per GPU-hour, while the RTX 5090 fell 9.2% from $0.92 to $0.84 — a spread that suggests demand may be shifting toward cost-efficient, mid-tier professional compute rather than peak single-GPU throughput. The B200 SXM's +6.3% move to $5.97 and the H100 SXM's smaller but directionally consistent +1.9% gain to $3.06 add a layer of complexity: frontier training-class silicon moved upward even as several A100 variants softened, with the A100 SXM 80GB slipping 2.2% to $1.88 and the A100 PCIe 80GB falling 2.4% to $3.38 across 18 reporting marketplaces.

Our weekly observations indicate that the L40 and L40S families are behaving differently from each other, with the L40 gaining 4.8% to $0.93 while the L40S showed a wide intra-family price range of $0.48 to $2.48 across 12 marketplaces — a spread that may reflect fragmented availability or significant configuration differences rather than a coherent demand signal. The A40 declined 4.6% to $0.75, moving in the same direction as the A100s, which may suggest softer demand in a specific workload tier, though with one week of data we cannot distinguish a sustained shift from a one-off redistribution of supply across the 29 reporting marketplaces.

Taken together, the cross-GPU pattern this week resists a single clean interpretation. The simultaneous rise in both very high-end SXM-class hardware and lower-cost professional SKUs like the RTX A4000, alongside weakness in the A100 family, could reflect multiple coexisting demand pools behaving independently. Ai Mining Co. tracked 7,300 observations across 109 distinct SKUs this week, and while that sample is broad, one week of divergent movement is insufficient to confirm whether these are structural separations between compute tiers or transient noise.

The company hasn’t publicly explained the increase, but the timing suggests a response to mounting demand for GPU-like processing power that underpins large-scale AI models. Competitors and customers are now scrambling to reassess their budgets and timelines.

Before the increase, SpaceX’s compute offerings were already considered a premium option for firms needing high-performance computing. The new pricing puts additional pressure on startups and research labs that rely on those resources to train and run their models.

5. Utilization Economics Favor Decentralization: Centralized GPU cloud providers operate at 60-70% GPU utilization, with the idle capacity gap absorbed into service pricing.

...

### Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud)

Hyperscalers bundle GPU access with hundreds of integrated cloud services, offering global reach and mature tooling suited to enterprises already running workloads inside their ecosystems. The tradeoff is premium per-hour pricing, vendor lock-in risk, and GPU queues that stretch months for reserved high-performance GPU compute capacity. This model fits teams where integration value with existing cloud services outweighs raw compute cost.

...

### On-Demand Pricing

On-demand GPU access charges hourly rates with no commitment, making it ideal for variable inference loads and short-horizon experimentation. Enterprise-grade hardware on centralized platforms runs $4.50-5.50 per H100 hour, compared to 40-80% lower rates on Aethir’s decentralized cloud network. Aethir’s H100 hourly price is up to 86% lower than Google Cloud's.

### Reserved Capacity

Reserved GPU contracts lock in capacity for 1-3 years in exchange for discounted pricing, typically 30-40% below on-demand rates. The risk is that demand forecasts are rarely accurate over multi-year horizons, leaving enterprises paying for idle GPU capacity during low-demand periods. This model suits teams with stable, predictable inference volume and multi-year budget visibility.

### Spot Compute

Spot GPU instances offer the lowest per-hour rates by using idle capacity, but carry preemption risk because the provider can reclaim the GPU with limited notice. Fault-tolerant batch jobs and non-latency-sensitive workloads can extract significant savings from spot pricing. Production inference pipelines and AI agents require guaranteed uptime and should not rely on spot availability.

### Egress Fees

Egress fees are data transfer charges applied when data exits a cloud provider's network, typically $0.09 per GB on hyperscaler platforms. At the inference scale, where models handle continuous input and output data streams, egress costs regularly add 15-30% to monthly GPU spend. Aethir charges no egress fees, which is a structural cost advantage for teams running high-throughput AI workloads.

Serverless inference is billed per token, not per GPU-hour, so if you're used to comparing GPU-hour rates, the apples-to-apples math against RunPod or Koyeb takes a beat. And if all you're doing is deploying one simple model, the full platform is more surface area than you strictly need. A GPU-focused specialist like RunPod might feel lighter.

#### Pricing 

Two tracks. Serverless inference is billed per token (same model as Together AI), starting at $0.05 per 1M tokens for smaller open-source models. For raw GPU compute, on-demand GPU Droplets are billed per second (5-minute minimum): L40S at $1.57/hr, H100 at $3.39/hr, H200 at $3.44/hr, and MI300X at $1.99/hr. (One gotcha: managed Dedicated Inference endpoints, which are fully hosted rather than self-managed Droplets, run higher, e.g. H100 around $4.41/hr. Different product, different number.) Full pricing details cover every hosted model and GPU tier.

Real talk: if I'm reaching past DigitalOcean, Cloudflare is probably my next call — and it's honestly not about the GPU specs. It's a brand I trust, the platform is developer-friendly, and the breadth of what surrounds the inference is hard to beat. You're not just renting a model endpoint; you're one config away from a CDN, KV store, queues, a vector database (Vectorize), and edge compute, all in the same place. For a lot of real apps, that ecosystem matters more than shaving a few cents off a GPU-hour.

Mechanically: Workers AI runs serverless inference across Cloudflare's edge network: 337 cities in 100+ countries, putting compute within ~50ms of 95% of internet users. It's per-request, so there are no idle costs and no GPU-hour billing. The trade: you work within Cloudflare's curated catalog of 50+ open-source models. You can run fine-tuned inference via your own LoRA adapters, but not self-host an arbitrary base model (private custom models are an enterprise/contact path).
